It is distinct from the definitive accent, which always falls on the final vowel of a word (2.3.2, 4.7.2.1). ... [p.35] Assigning levels of stress is complicated by the overlay of phrase stress (2.3.3).

4568.heavy: A syllable containing a long vowel (a sequence of two like vowels, including across a morpheme boundary) or a rising diphthong (/ai, au/ most commonly; also /ei, eu, ae, ao, oi, ou/; level sequences /eo, oe, io/ normally behave alike, /iu, ui/ variably). Falling vowel sequences /ia, ua, ie, ue, ea, oa, uo/ are not stress units. The language has no closed syllables.
4568.dflt: Penultimate mora, i.e. penultimate syllable of an all-light word, with alternating secondary stress on every second syllable leftward (source: 'This rule correctly predicts the stress placement on a word with any number of syllables of the form CV'; examples paka, pepeke, winangalo, mangamanga, Kilitimeti).
4568.prule: Mora-counting rule: stress falls on the vowel of the penultimate mora of the word and on every second mora to its left. A long vowel (two like vowels) or a rising diphthong is bimoraic and takes stress as a unit on its first vowel (stress shifted back to the syllable start if the count lands on its second mora); no two successive morae are stressed. Primary stress falls on the syllable containing a long vowel or rising diphthong (a long vowel outranks a rising diphthong; with two such syllables the first is marginally stronger); if the word has none, primary stress is on the penultimate mora (= penultimate syllable in all-light words). Falling vowel sequences /ia ua ie ue ea oa uo/ count as two separate morae, so word-final stress arises on words ending in a long vowel or rising diphthong (akalaa, manamanataa).
4568.srule: Secondary stresses are the non-primary positions of the penultimate-mora count: the penultimate mora and every second mora to its left are stressed (long vowels and rising diphthongs as units; each morpheme of a complex word counted separately), the primary being the one on a long-vowel or rising-diphthong syllable, else the penultimate mora; the others are secondary, preceding the primary in all-light or final-heavy words (lòtotónu, màtawíti, àkaláa, mànamànatáa) and falling on the penultimate mora when the primary is on an earlier heavy syllable (máalàma, uwáilèti).

4568.tone: The grammar describes no tone system: the suprasegmental chapter (2.3) covers only word stress (2.3.1), the definitive accent (2.3.2) and pause/phrase stress (2.3.3), and 'tone' never occurs as a phonological term (a full-text search of the thesis finds only 'emotional in tone', 'Tone' as a place-name gloss, and 'tone group'), so 'no tone' is an inference from the source's silence, not a stated denial. The 'definitive accent' (sec. 2.3.2) is a grammatical accent on the final vowel of a definite noun phrase (added mora of length, optional pitch rise), explicitly distinguished from word stress.

This mobility allows words to be stressed in two ways: in the first, stress falls on the last syllable of a word in isolation or of a word used at the end of a phrase. 4581.heavy: Not stated. 4581.prule: No fixed position. Clairis 1977: stress tends to fall on the penultimate syllable, but there are exceptions and its place cannot always be predicted; in many cases the accent can be moved without the informant taking notice, and units were often heard with no syllable (or every syllable) prominent. Aguilera 1978: stress is 'libre', falling on any of the last three syllables of uninflected (thematic) forms and shifting in suffixed (compound) forms; Aguilera's promised placement rules were never published in any reachable source. Salas 1996 (after Aguilera 1982/83): free over the last three syllables, non-contrastive (esdrújula/grave/aguda all keep the same meaning). Hence free, non-contrastive variation in placement within a right-edge window, with a penultimate tendency at most.

4582.dq: In Kemant, all words have stress in isolation, but some may lose it in context.
4582.prule: No placement rule stated by any reachable source. Kemant is affirmed as a stress language (not tone): every word carries stress in isolation, some words lose it in context; plural suffixes attract stress. Appleyard (1991) hedges that the system 'may have moved, or be moving towards a predictable, syllable-counting stress-based system' but names no syllable. The two Addis Ababa theses (Tsige 2009, Zelealem 2000) treat only gemination and vowel length under 'Suprasegmentals' and say nothing about stress.

4587.heavy: 'long syllable' = syllable with a long kernel (vowel peak); Robbins 1961 distinguishes short and long syllables, free or checked (§3.22, Figure 2, pp. 247-248) and only length counts for stress, not checkedness. Vowel length is phonemic in the language: Castillo 2012: 134-136 reanalyses Robbins 1968's 'ballistic vs controlled' accent as exactly this short/long vowel contrast ('el contraste no es silábico, sino segmental'). 4587.dflt: a short syllable with a tone glide; else whichever of the first two syllables carries the higher tone; else (identical tones on the first two syllables) the second syllable
4587.prule: Predictable word stress, stated with hedges ('seems to be predictable', 'normally', 'on the basis of the evidence so far observed'): the first (leftmost) long syllable in the word is stressed; if there is no long syllable, a short syllable with a tone glide (contour tone) is stressed; failing both, whichever of the first two syllables carries the higher tone; if the first two syllables carry identical tones (no long syllable, no glide), the second syllable. Words are mostly monosyllabic (Castillo 2012: 100); the rule applies to polysyllabic words (Robbins' examples are a person-inflected verb form 'I'll ask', 'beans', and compounds 'bread', 'sea', 'singer').
4587.srule: None: one stress per word -- 'A word consists of one or more syllables, only one of which is stressed' (Gardner & Merrifield 1990: 92); pretonic (prefixal) and posttonic (reduced-pronoun, modal) syllables are unstressed. tn.quote: 12.1 . Three level tones, High, Mid, Low are found in all the dialects studied . and usually they correspond without change . … A fourth tone, High to Low Fall, has been recor- ded in many of the dialects . The position for this tone in Pro- to - Mumuye is not clear 23 … tone marks, High and Low`, and two combina- tions of them High - Low Fall and Low - High Rise ', should be used, for a Mumuye text to be fully intelligible . Mid tone can be left unmarked . The two contour tones are indispensable in order to mark the verb tenses accurately .
